subsection: 10. Literature and social criticism, East and West; changing patterns in religious observance

notes.h: Background: censorship, the Gulag and the thaw
notes.b: To understand why writers mattered so much in this period, you need to know what they were up against. In the communist states writing was a political act, and in the West the Cold War shaped what intellectuals argued about.
points: Stalin's terror (the 1930s to his death in 1953) filled the Gulag, the Soviet system of labour camps, so the camps were a fact of life that the state did not want discussed.

In 1956 Khrushchev, Stalin's successor, denounced Stalin's crimes in his secret speech. The loosening of controls that followed is called the thaw, and it made the 1962 publication of One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich possible.

Communist states controlled publishing and the press through censorship and the official Writers' Unions, and the KGB (the Soviet secret police) policed dissent, so a writer who criticised the system risked losing the right to publish, prison or exile.
A dissident writer is a writer who openly opposed a communist state's policy or ideology and faced censorship, prison or exile as a result.
The Cold War divided Europe, and Western intellectuals argued fiercely over communism, the USA and colonialism, which is why many Western writers of this period took political sides.

Before 1945 Western Europe was largely Christian in practice, whereas the communist parties in the East were officially atheist, so religion was a matter of habit in the West and of conflict with the state in the East.
notes.tip: Examiners accept a definition of dissident writer only if it is tied to censorship, the camps or exile. Saying only that the writer disagreed with the system does not earn the mark.

notes.h: Key personality: Alexander Solzhenitsyn (camps and first fame)
notes.b: Solzhenitsyn was the Soviet novelist whose writing on the Gulag made the camp system known to the world and made him the most famous dissident in the Soviet Union. His own years as a prisoner gave him his subject.
points: He was born in Kislovodsk on 11 December 1918 and served as an artillery officer (a captain) in the Red Army in the Second World War.
In February 1945 he was arrested at the front for criticising Stalin in private letters to a friend, which shows how far the terror reached, since even private remarks were punished.

He was sentenced to eight years in labour camps and then to internal exile (forced residence inside the USSR) in Kazakhstan from 1953. The exile ended in 1956, so he spent eight years in camps and about three in exile.
In 1954 he was treated for cancer in a hospital in Tashkent and was cured, an episode that lies behind his novel Cancer Ward.
One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich appeared in the Soviet journal Novy Mir in November 1962 with Khrushchev's personal approval, which was possible because of the thaw.

The novel describes a single day of a camp prisoner, Ivan Denisovich Shukhov, in a Stalin-era camp. It brought the camps into Soviet public discussion because it was an officially approved publication.

After Khrushchev fell in October 1964 censorship tightened, so The First Circle and Cancer Ward could be published only abroad, in 1968, and he was expelled from the Soviet Writers' Union in November 1969.
He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970, but he did not travel to receive it, fearing that he would not be allowed back into the USSR.
notes.tip: Always give the year of each work and keep the two Solzhenitsyn expulsions apart: the Writers' Union expulsion (1969) is not the expulsion from the country (1974). His eight years in camps (1945 to 1953) are also different from the exile in Kazakhstan (1953 to 1956).

notes.h: Key personality: Alexander Solzhenitsyn (the Gulag Archipelago and exile)
notes.b: Once his official publishing stopped, Solzhenitsyn wrote the book that made him an enemy of the state. Its publication abroad led straight to his expulsion, and he continued to write and speak from exile.
points: The Gulag Archipelago is non-fiction: a work of testimony, history and reflection on the camp system, drawing on the accounts of many prisoners. Unlike Ivan Denisovich, it was banned in the USSR.
The KGB seized a copy of the manuscript in 1973, and this led him to authorise publication. It appeared in Paris at the end of 1973 and had a major impact in the West.
He was arrested on 12 February 1974 and flown the next day to West Germany, where he was stripped of his citizenship. The expulsion therefore followed the Archipelago, not Ivan Denisovich.
In exile he lived first in West Germany, then in Switzerland, and from 1976 in Vermont in the USA.
In his Harvard commencement address of June 1978 he criticised Western materialism and weakness as well as communism, which disappointed many of his Western admirers.
From Vermont he continued to write The Red Wheel, his multi-volume historical cycle on the Russian Revolution.
He returned to Russia in 1994 and died in Moscow in August 2008.
notes.tip: Exams reward linking each event to its consequence: the KGB seizure of the manuscript led to publication in Paris, publication led to his arrest and expulsion in 1974. Keep the novel (1962, approved) separate from the non-fiction book (1973, banned).

notes.h: Key personality: Alexander Solzhenitsyn (why he is a dissident writer, and how he is judged)
notes.b: Solzhenitsyn fits the definition of a dissident writer exactly, and both his contemporaries and later historians judged him in divided ways.
points: He is a dissident writer because he opposed the Soviet system through his writing, exposing the camps that the state wanted hidden, and he was punished for it with censorship, expulsion from the Writers' Union and exile.
The Soviet authorities called him a traitor and expelled him, while many Western intellectuals admired him, though some later disliked his nationalist and religious views.

Historians regard his work as central to Western understanding of Soviet terror, because he gave the West evidence from the inside, although some question the reliability of his testimony and his later political stances.
In Russia after 1994 his reputation was divided between admirers who saw him as the nation's conscience and critics who disliked his Russian nationalism and his religious conservatism.
notes.tip: If you are asked to judge him, use the pairs: traitor to the Soviet authorities and hero to many in the West; essential witness to historians but with questions over his testimony and later politics.

notes.h: Key personality: Simone de Beauvoir (writer and critic: journal, novels and memoirs)
notes.b: Beauvoir (1908-1986) is best known for The Second Sex, but she was also a novelist, memoirist and critic who questioned Western society and its values from the Paris intellectual left. Here she is the writer and critic.
points: In 1945 she joined Jean-Paul Sartre in founding the review Les Temps modernes, which became the leading journal of left-wing intellectuals in France.
Her novel The Mandarins portrayed the Parisian intellectual left after the Second World War and won the Prix Goncourt, a leading French literary prize, in 1954.
Her memoirs, including Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter (1958), described her youth, and they also describe her relationship with Sartre.
That relationship was a lifelong partnership by choice without marriage. Admirers presented it as a model of equality, while critics called it a privilege of the elite.
When Sartre died in 1980 she wrote about his death in Adieux: A Farewell to Sartre (1981).
Her essay La vieillesse (The Coming of Age, 1970) attacked the way society treated the elderly, so her criticism reached beyond politics to everyday attitudes.
The Second Sex (1949), which described women as defined as the Other, made her a founder of modern feminism.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph, give the dated points: Les Temps modernes (1945), The Mandarins (Goncourt, 1954), the memoirs (1958) and her political causes. Mention The Second Sex only briefly as a link rather than retelling it.

notes.h: Key personality: Simone de Beauvoir (politics, travels and how she is judged)
notes.b: Beauvoir used her reputation to take public stands, especially over Algeria, and her view of communism changed as she saw it at first hand.
points: She took part in the political debates of the 1960s and 1970s, supporting the left and speaking out for the rights of women and of prisoners.
In September 1960 she signed the Manifesto of the 121, which supported French conscripts who refused to fight in the Algerian war.
She campaigned against torture by the French army and in 1962 championed the case of Djamila Boupacha, an Algerian woman who alleged torture by French forces.
With Sartre she visited the Soviet Union, China (1955) and Cuba (1960), where she observed communism at first hand, and her views on it changed over time.
Contemporaries praised her as a writer and public intellectual, while conservative critics attacked her for challenging traditional morality.
Historians now judge her as one of the most influential critics of the twentieth century, though her later political views are contested.
notes.tip: Strong answers connect her to events: Les Temps modernes, the Algerian war and the 1954 Goncourt. Remember the contrast with Solzhenitsyn: she was free to publish and was attacked in debate.

notes.b: Writers in the communist states could not publish freely, so they found other ways to reach readers. They circulated unofficial copies, sent work abroad and relied on Western radio to carry banned works back.
points: Samizdat (Russian for self-published) was the system by which typed and copied manuscripts were passed from hand to hand in the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia. The authors' work could thus circulate without passing the censor.
Some writers instead smuggled their work abroad to be published there. Western radio stations such as Radio Free Europe and the BBC then broadcast banned works to the East.
Boris Pasternak's Doctor Zhivago was first published in Italy in 1957. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958 and, under pressure from the Soviet authorities, declined it.

In 1966 Andrei Sinyavsky and Yuli Daniel were sentenced to labour camps (seven and five years) for publishing satires abroad under pseudonyms, and in 1964 Joseph Brodsky was tried for social parasitism. Both cases drew international protest.
Andrei Sakharov, the physicist central to the Soviet hydrogen bomb, became a human rights campaigner. He was exiled to Gorky in January 1980 and released in December 1986 under Gorbachev.
Dissident writers faced expulsion, imprisonment or exile, and Solzhenitsyn's expulsion in 1974 was the most famous example.
notes.tip: Keep the Nobel Prizes straight: Pasternak (1958, declined under pressure), Solzhenitsyn (1970, accepted) and Sartre (1964, refused by choice) are different cases.

notes.h: Eastern dissidents: Czechoslovakia, Poland and the Helsinki Final Act
notes.b: Outside the Soviet Union, writers in Czechoslovakia and Poland also challenged the state. In the 1970s international agreements gave dissidents a new standard to appeal to.
points: Milan Kundera's novel The Joke (1967) and the Czechoslovak Writers' Union congress of June 1967, which criticised censorship, were part of the intellectual ferment that came before the Prague Spring of 1968.
Václav Havel, a Czech playwright, wrote The Power of the Powerless in 1978. He argued that ordinary people could resist by "living within the truth", as it is reported.

Havel helped to found Charter 77, a human rights manifesto of January 1977, and he was imprisoned from 1979 and released in early 1983, so most of 1979-83 was spent in jail. He became president of Czechoslovakia in December 1989.
Polish writers also took part: Czesław Miłosz, who defected in 1951, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1980, the same year as Solidarity's rise.

The Helsinki Final Act of 1975, in which the signatories (the USSR included) accepted human rights commitments, gave dissidents a standard of rights to appeal to, since their government had signed it.
notes.tip: Date Havel's The Power of the Powerless as 1978 only, and use Charter 77 and his imprisonment as the link between his writing and his later presidency.

notes.h: Western social criticism: totalitarianism and conformity
notes.b: Social criticism means writing that attacks the faults of a society. Western writers were free to publish, and they used that freedom to criticise totalitarianism (a state that controls every part of life) and the conformity of their own societies.
points: George Orwell's Animal Farm (1945) and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) criticised Stalinism and the abuse of power, and both became standard texts in the Cold War.
Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) was read alongside Nineteen Eighty-Four as a warning against conformity and totalitarian control, whether communist or consumerist.
Albert Camus's The Plague (1947) used an epidemic as an allegory (a story with a hidden political meaning) for resistance to tyranny, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.
Camus broke with Sartre in 1952, after his book The Rebel (1951), over the question of communism and violence. He was killed in a car crash in January 1960.
notes.tip: Remember the distinction between the two kinds of writer: Eastern dissident writers risked prison, while Western social critics were free to publish and criticised society.

notes.h: Western social criticism: existentialism, Germany and Britain
notes.b: In France, Germany and Britain, writers also turned their criticism on their own societies, on their national pasts and on class.
points: Jean-Paul Sartre's existentialism, expressed in Being and Nothingness (1943) and in his plays, argued that people are free and responsible for their choices. It dominated French thought in the late 1940s and 1950s.
Sartre's plays and essays also criticised bourgeois society (the comfortable middle class) and colonialism, and in 1964 he declined the Nobel Prize in Literature by his own choice.
Günter Grass's The Tin Drum (1959) examined Germany's wartime past and the moral compromises of ordinary people, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1999.
Heinrich Böll's novels criticised the restoration of West German society after 1945 and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1972.
In Britain, John Osborne's play Look Back in Anger (1956) and the writers known as the Angry Young Men attacked class and complacency in post-war society.
notes.tip: Sartre refused the Nobel Prize (1964) by choice, unlike Pasternak, who declined under pressure. Examiners expect you to name the work and its year.

notes.h: Secularisation and falling church attendance in the West
notes.b: Secularisation means religion losing belief, practice and influence in public life. In much of Western Europe it advanced quickly from the 1960s, and the authority of the churches over everyday life declined.
points: Attendance at Mass and other religious services fell in most Western European countries from the 1960s, and the fall was sharpest among young people.
There were national differences: attendance fell sharply in Britain, the Netherlands, France and Scandinavia, while in Ireland and Poland religious practice remained high for longer.
The Netherlands is a striking case, because Catholic Mass attendance fell dramatically between the 1960s and 1980s and many left the Church.
Secularisation meant that the state, education and family life increasingly ran without reference to religious authority.
The decline of clergy vocations (people choosing to become priests, monks or nuns) was visible by the 1970s, when seminaries and religious orders in many countries recruited far fewer men and women.
notes.tip: A common question asks you to name two reasons church attendance fell, so learn the causes of secularisation and use named examples such as the Netherlands.

notes.h: Causes of secularisation, and divisions in the Catholic Church
notes.b: No single event caused the decline of religion. Several social changes worked together, and the Catholic Church was also divided from inside.
points: Rising affluence and growing education were causes of secularisation.
Television brought new ideas and entertainment into the home, and urban life loosened the close communities in which church attendance had been a habit.
The welfare state took over services once run by the churches, so people needed the church less.
In the 1960s people questioned authority of all kinds, including the authority of the churches, and this was one cause of secularisation.
The reforms of the Second Vatican Council (a Catholic Church council) and the controversy over contraception created divisions in the Church.
In Humanae Vitae (July 1968) Pope Paul VI reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception, which many Catholics found hard to accept.
notes.tip: Name at least two causes and give a reason for each; examiners also credit the Netherlands, Humanae Vitae and a West-East comparison.

notes.b: While Christian practice declined, migration brought a new religion into Western Europe. It made religion visible in public life again in societies that were becoming more secular.
points: Muslim communities grew in Western Europe through migration from North Africa (especially to France), Turkey (especially to West Germany) and South Asia (especially to Britain).
These communities set up prayer rooms and mosques, so a new religion became a visible part of many European cities.
notes.tip: Mention Islam as a further change alongside secularisation. Name the migrant groups and where they settled rather than just saying immigration.

notes.b: In the East, churches faced persecution or state control rather than the gradual decline seen in the West. Some, however, kept real influence and became centres of resistance.
points: The Catholic Church in Czechoslovakia was suppressed after the communist takeover of 1948, and bishops were imprisoned.

In Poland the Church retained real independence and mass support. Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński was interned from 1953 to 1956, but its influence grew after the election of the Polish pope, Karol Wojtyła (John Paul II), in 1978.

In Hungary Cardinal József Mindszenty was arrested in December 1948 and sentenced to life imprisonment in February 1949. He was freed in the uprising of October 1956 and took refuge in the US legation in Budapest from November 1956 until 1971, about 15 years.
The Evangelical (Protestant) Church in East Germany adopted a policy of coexistence with the state while maintaining its own institutions and social work.
In East Germany church-led peace prayers in Leipzig in autumn 1989 preceded the mass demonstrations, so the churches provided a protected space where protest could begin.
The Russian Orthodox Church was permitted to operate under tight state control and KGB infiltration. Khrushchev's anti-religious campaign of 1959-64 closed thousands of churches.
The contrast with the West is that religion in the East was persecuted or controlled by the state, whereas in the West it declined by voluntary choice.
notes.tip: Keep secularisation (a decline of religion in society) apart from persecution (a state policy). Credit goes to a structure that compares West and East and to named examples such as Mindszenty, Wyszyński and Leipzig.

notes.b: The ecumenical movement means cooperation and moves towards unity among Christian churches of different denominations. After 1945, as Christian practice fell in the West, the churches cooperated more closely than at any time since the Reformation.
points: The World Council of Churches was founded at Amsterdam in August 1948 by Protestant, Anglican and Orthodox churches. The Roman Catholic Church did not join, and the Russian Orthodox Church joined in 1961.
Taizé, an ecumenical community in Burgundy, France, founded in 1940 by Brother Roger (Roger Schutz), drew young people from many countries in the 1960s and 1970s.
In January 1964 Pope Paul VI met Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople in Jerusalem, a step towards reconciling the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
In December 1965 the mutual excommunications of 1054, by which the two churches had condemned each other, were lifted.
notes.tip: If asked what the ecumenical movement aimed at, say cooperation and unity among Christian churches, and support it with the World Council of Churches (and the fact that Catholics did not join) and the 1964 meeting.

notes.b: Historians debate how far writers and religious movements shaped political change and how far they merely reflected it. The judgement is balanced on both sides.
points: Achievement: dissident writing kept the truth about Stalin's crimes alive and gave the West evidence, which helped to create an intellectual opposition in the communist states.
Limit: samizdat had a small readership, and most citizens were not directly reached by dissident writing, so the regimes survived until 1989-91 for other reasons.
Contemporaries: Soviet authorities called Solzhenitsyn a traitor, while many in the West praised dissident writers as heroes of freedom.

Later views: historians rate Solzhenitsyn and Beauvoir as hugely influential, though his testimony and politics and her later political views are questioned. Beauvoir was praised by contemporaries and attacked by conservative critics.
Religion: secularisation in the West was a broad social trend with several causes, not the result of a single event or movement.
In the East, religion was a source of resistance in Poland and East Germany, which is the reverse of the Western trend.
notes.tip: Build the judgement as paired points, such as achievements against limits, and contemporary against later views, so that your essay argues a thesis and does not just list facts.

keyTerms.definition: A writer who openly opposed the official policies or ideology of a communist state, often facing censorship, imprisonment or exile.
The movement among Christian churches to cooperate and reunite across denominational divisions, formally organised in the World Council of Churches.
The unofficial, self-published and hand-copied literature circulated in the Soviet Union and other communist states.
The decline of religious belief, practice and influence in public life as society becomes less religious.
The Soviet system of labour camps and prisons in which millions were held under Stalin, and the subject of Solzhenitsyn's work.
Writing that examines and condemns the moral and political condition of a society, as the work of Orwell and Camus did.
The philosophy, associated with Sartre and de Beauvoir, that people are free and must take responsibility for their choices.
British writers of the 1950s, including John Osborne, who attacked class privilege and complacency in post-war society.
A system in which the state controls all aspects of life, the target of Orwell's novels.
